chapter_theme: King Saccandan, unable to leave Queen Vijayai, hands the guarding of his kingdom to his minister Kattiyankaran; a soothsayer and the counsellor Rudradattan warn him, the second with exempla of gods and heroes shamed by lust, but the king answers that past penance measures his joys and goes back to his pleasures, which the narrator ascribes both to a sprouting past destiny and to his own heart. That night Vijayai sees three frightening dreams and at dawn worships the god and then her husband.

cast.role: Saccandan's minister, to whom he hands the rule
a soothsayer who warns the king
a minister who counsels the king against his absorption in pleasure

198.reading: The king, slipping from his guard of the land and bound to his rare jewel of a woman, is likened to the white moon hiding with Rohini while the sky goes dark.
198.nuance: The simile is double-edged: the moon with its favourite star is a stock image of love, but here the moon's hiding leaves the sky dark, so the land's darkening is folded into the praise of the lovers.
198.event: Saccandan gives himself to Vijayai and lets slip his watch over the kingdom.

199.reading: While the saffron-shouldered king and the fish-eyed queen drink the flood of their love without pause, the poet announces that he will now tell plainly how fortune slipped from the king of the white umbrella.
199.nuance: The narrator frames the love scene as the start of a fall before any counsel is given, so the reader hears the warnings that follow already knowing they will fail.

200.reading: Among the king's ministers was one called Kattiyankaran, who was to the king as his own life; the king had his honour proclaimed by drum and, taking this man of sound learning aside, spoke to him.
200.nuance: Kattiyankaran is introduced with praise, உயிர் என ஒழுகும் and வெளிறு இலாக் கேள்வி, that the story will turn against him; the narrator does not yet hint at his treachery.
200.event: Saccandan honours Kattiyankaran publicly and takes him aside to speak.

201.reading: The king says he cannot bear to part from Vijayai, the faultless woman who came to him by a boon and is like nectar, and asks Kattiyankaran to become king and guard the world so that it sings his fame.
201.nuance: The king does not abdicate in name; he hands over the work of guarding (காத்தல்) while keeping the crown, which is the split of office and power the soothsayer warns against in 204.
201.event: Saccandan asks Kattiyankaran to rule in his place so that he need not leave Vijayai.

202.reading: Kattiyankaran, hearing the lord, protests that his guarding the wide world would be like laying the painted seat of a war elephant's neck on a dog, and the king tells him not to refuse.
202.nuance: The verse holds two speeches without naming the first speaker; reading the dog simile as Kattiyankaran's self-abasement and line 4 as the king's insistence fits the நீ of line 4 and the அண்ணல் of line 1. His modesty here sets up the reversal of 241.
202.event: Kattiyankaran demurs, and Saccandan insists that he accept.

203.reading: When the king had spoken, Kattiyankaran bowed at his feet and said: let the king enjoy to the full his love for the one he loves, and he himself will wear the yoke of guarding the world so that no blame falls on it.
203.event: Kattiyankaran accepts the rule and promises to guard the land without blame.

204.reading: When the king sent him off and Kattiyankaran took charge of the army, a soothsayer told the king, by the rule of his craft, that if he set sovereignty upon one man, prosperity would leave the land.
204.nuance: The warning is about concentration of power, not about Kattiyankaran's character; the story bears it out when he plots against the king (241), which is why the claim is marked asserted.
204.event: Kattiyankaran takes command of the army, and a soothsayer warns the king against giving power to one man.

claims.claim: a king who sets his sovereignty upon a single man drives prosperity from his land

205.reading: The king answers that the man is called his life, has no one but him, has melted the enemy's front and won many battles; he has done for him what he should, let the man do what he should, and no one is to speak words that grieve his mind; go, and long life to you.
205.nuance: The king's grounds for trust are affection and past service in war, not a testing of the man for rule; and his ban on words that grieve the mind is the very closing-off of rebuke that the ministers try to break through next.
205.event: Saccandan dismisses the soothsayer, vouching for Kattiyankaran's loyalty and victories.

206.reading: A counsellor asks the guardian to hear graciously, even if it is not his wish: those who take the word of the learned meet only good and never harm, and many who sank in pleasure with creeper-like women also met sin and blame.
206.nuance: பாவமும் பழியும் pairs a moral fault with public disgrace; the examples that follow (207 to 211) argue almost wholly from disgrace, the blame that outlives the deed. The speaker is named only in 212; that 206 to 212 are one speech is read from the run of என்றான் endings.
206.event: A minister, later named Rudradattan, begins to counsel the king against his absorption in pleasure.

claims.claim: those who follow the counsel of the learned meet only good
those who sink in pleasure with women incur sin and blame

207.reading: Brahma, great of name, desired a girl whose breasts were budding so that four faces grew on him to see her; he lost his place in heaven and, though he mended his ways, the small talk about him stands to this day.
207.nuance: A counsellor in a Jain epic draws his exempla of lust from the Brahmanical gods, which serves both as warning and as a quiet slight on those gods; the point made is that blame outlasts amendment (திருந்தினாற்கு).

208.reading: For the one with the konrai garland and the cool moon on his head, taking as half of himself the dark-haired daughter of the mountain king became a mark and a great blame.
208.nuance: The form in which Siva shares his body with Uma, which Saiva texts praise, is here counted as a மறு, a stain like the moon's. This is the counsellor's polemical reading, one a Saiva reader would not accept.

209.reading: The dark-hued one once stole the women's long garments, and, seeing that this was blameworthy in the eyes of his white-hued elder, broke a kurundu tree in the Yamuna for the bangled women.
209.nuance: The episode is Krishna's theft of the herdswomen's clothes; what the breaking of the kurundu tree does in this telling (giving the women cover, or an act of shame before Balarama) the verse does not make plain.

210.reading: When a lust-burnt she-ass was seen, one called Vamana went to her out of pity and joined with her, and the world cast him off like a garland from the pyre, saying he had brought suffering on himself; this is what we learn, O king.
210.nuance: Who வாமனார் is here, and which story is meant, cannot be fixed from the verse; the grim irony is that arul, compassion, is named as the motive of a lustful act.

211.reading: Can great blame be hidden? Who can wipe out the scar-word the Pandavas earned, which the world beat out like a drum? Lust brings disgrace and more besides; to stand fair and guard the world seems the good course.
211.nuance: நல்லதே போலும் is softened to 'seems good', a courtier's tact before a king who has forbidden grieving words.

claims.claim: the blame that lust brings cannot be hidden and spreads through the world
a king's good lies in standing impartial and guarding the world

212.reading: Even thousand-eyed Indra, who never scorns wisdom, follows the word of the sharp-minded; you too are of great wisdom, yet you have one single thought that will bring grief to your doe-like queen, said Rudradattan.
212.nuance: ஓர் அறிவு plays against பேர் அறிவு: 'one thought' but also 'one sense', the lowest rank of living beings in the Jain scheme of one- to five-sensed lives, so the king of great wisdom is told he lives like a one-sensed creature. The pun is a reading; the plain sense stands without it.
212.event: Rudradattan closes his counsel by warning that the king's single-minded passion will bring the queen grief.

claims.claim: even the greatest ruler should be led by the counsel of the wise

213.reading: The jewelled king replies that for those who guarded a measured, rare penance, all their pleasures are measured out to each of them that very day, and so are the days they live; let no one tell him this.
213.nuance: The king turns the doctrine that past deeds measure present joy into a reason not to listen. The narrator also speaks of past destiny (215), but the work does not endorse its use as an excuse: the minister of 233, later in this ilampakam, names his fall as his own lapse into the wrong path.
213.event: Saccandan rejects the counsel, saying his pleasures and lifespan were fixed by past penance.

claims.claim: the pleasures and the lifespan one enjoys are measured out by the penance of a former life

214.reading: Rudradattan says that, even if the king is angry, he spoke looking to his good, having seen that this is the way of the subtle books of dharma; let the king embrace the young breasts of the fragrant-garlanded woman as his feast; he himself will go.
214.nuance: The parting line can be read as resigned leave or as bitter irony; either way the counsellor withdraws rather than presses.
214.event: Rudradattan defends his counsel as dharma, bids the king enjoy the queen, and leaves the court.

claims.claim: a counsellor must speak for his king's good even at the risk of the king's anger, as the books of dharma direct

215.reading: Though told it was harm, the king took no thought of danger, because a destiny formed before sprouted and rose in him, and he ran the way his heart led to the woman with flower-decked hair.
215.nuance: Karma and the king's own heart are both given as the cause in one verse: முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை sprouts, and the king runs மனமாம் நெறி. The narrator does not let destiny excuse him; the minister of 233 blames his choice.
215.event: Saccandan ignores all warning and follows his desire for Vijayai.

claims.claim: a destiny formed in the past sprouts and drives a man past every warning

216.reading: Without wearying of her girdle-clad hips and her breast, the king of the jewelled chest drank the nectar of unfailing fortune and rejoiced.
216.nuance: உலையாத் திரு, 'unfailing fortune', is ironic after 199 has told that fortune is about to slip away.
216.event: Saccandan gives himself wholly to pleasure with Vijayai.

217.reading: Revelling so that gems scattered from his crown, the king and the jewelled queen became like the Nagas of rare jewels.
217.event: Saccandan gives himself wholly to pleasure with Vijayai.

218.reading: In the darkness of their pleasure, like a bright gem fallen into a young honey-filled lotus, the spear-eyed queen dreamed.
218.nuance: Line 3 (அறவு ஆக்கிய இன்பம்) is hard to construe; the image of the gem in the lotus may stand for the king in the queen's embrace or for the child she will conceive.
218.event: Vijayai dreams in the night beside the king.

219.reading: Coral-lipped and soft-footed, she saw three dreams as she slept, and trembled with fear; meanwhile the hot sun rose and it was dawn.
219.event: Vijayai sees three dreams, wakes trembling, and dawn breaks.

220.reading: With soft fingers that know the lute the queen washed her eyes, put on her garments, and worshipped the feet of the great lord of famed bounty, who bears the conquering wheel and on whom the sky rains flowers.
220.nuance: மால் can name Vishnu, but the wheel (நேமி) and the rain of flowers from the sky are marks of the Jina in Jain praise; the god is read as the Jina on those marks.
220.event: Vijayai rises, dresses and worships the Lord's feet.

221.reading: Bringing flowers not of this world and sandal paste, praising, 'let them reach the feet of our lord', she then went to the feet of her own lord.
221.nuance: The verse sets எம் பெருமான் அடி (the god's feet) and தம் பெருமான் அடி (her husband's feet) in parallel lines, giving the wife's day an order: the god first, then the husband.
221.event: Vijayai makes her offering to the god and then goes to her husband.

links.note: The soothsayer warns that setting power on one man will drive prosperity from the land; in 241 Kattiyankaran, now holding that power, says a deity urges him night and day to kill the king.
links.teaches: The prophecy names no traitor, only the structure of power, so its fulfilment shows the epic locating the danger in the king's act of delegation before it locates it in the minister's character.

links.note: Kattiyankaran bows and promises to bear the yoke so that no blame falls on the land; in 241 he asks his council how to kill the king, laying the impulse on a hostile deity.
links.teaches: The minister who vowed blameless guardianship later disowns his own intent by blaming a god, so the story pairs the king's excuse by destiny (213) with the usurper's excuse by possession.

links.note: Vijayai's three dreams, which leave her trembling at dawn, are told in 223: the ashoka tree falls and a sprout rises from its root.
links.teaches: The dream that frightens her is a dream of fall and succession, and when the king reads it (225) he speaks only of the heir and keeps silent on the fall, so her fear at 219 rightly answers the half that is withheld.

links.note: The narrator says past destiny sprouted and the king followed his heart; the minister of 233 tells the king he left the path of justice and bathed in the liquor of lust.
links.teaches: The epic gives the king's fall two causes in two voices, destiny in the narrator's and the king's own wrong path in the minister's, and does not let either cancel the other.

links.note: Both queens wake from dreams of the king's fall: the Pandya queen sees umbrella and sceptre drop; Vijayai's dream (told in 223) shows the tree that is the king falling and a sprout rising.
links.teaches: The Silappathikaram's queen dreams only the end of a reign, while the Cintamani's queen dreams an end that carries an heir, so the same omen-form serves tragedy in one epic and a story of restoration in the other.

links.note: Kural 377 says even the rich enjoy only as the apportioner has apportioned; the king says his pleasures and life-days are measured by past penance and so refuses counsel.
links.teaches: The couplet's limit on enjoyment becomes, in a king's mouth, a licence to stop listening, which shows that a doctrine of allotted fruit can be turned against the duty to act on advice.

gains.a: the king's refusal is seen to borrow a recognised ethical teaching rather than being bare infatuation
gains.b: the couplet is shown to be open to a fatalist misuse it does not itself guard against

links.note: Kural 509 bids a ruler trust no one unexamined; the king vouches for Kattiyankaran by love and past victories and forbids further words.
links.teaches: Loyalty and battle service, the very grounds the king gives, are not the examination the couplet asks for, so the scene shows how trust can feel tested while skipping the test of fitness for power.

gains.a: the king's grounds for trust are measured against a stated rule and found to fall short of it
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'examine' is shown failing in a case where the examiner thinks he already knows the man

links.note: Kural 448 says a king without rebukers perishes even with no enemy; the king hears Rudradattan's rebuke, rejects it, and the counsellor withdraws.
links.teaches: The epic shows the middle case the couplet skips, a king who has a rebuker and sends him away, and its ruin comes through the trusted man, so the danger lies in refusing rebuke as much as in lacking it.

gains.a: the counsellor's failure is given the weight of a known rule of kingship
gains.b: the couplet's 'having no rebuker' is shown to include a king who drives rebuke off

links.note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; the narrator says the king followed his heart to the queen because a past destiny sprouted.
links.teaches: The couplet treats being led by desire for one's wife as a fault to be avoided, while the epic adds a ripening past deed as its cause, which raises the question the couplet does not face: whether such a man could have chosen otherwise.

gains.a: the king's surrender to desire is named as a recognised fault of rulers, not only a love story
gains.b: the couplet's simple prohibition is set against a story where karma also pushes the man

links.note: Kural 55 praises the wife who rises worshipping her husband and not a god; Vijayai rises, worships the god's feet, and then goes to her lord's feet.
links.teaches: A Jain epic keeps the wife's devotion to her husband but sets worship of the god first, so the couplet's exclusive ranking is answered with an order of two duties rather than a choice between them.

gains.a: the queen's morning is seen as a deliberate ordering of devotions against a known ideal
gains.b: the couplet's 'not a god' is shown to be a position a later work could decline while still honouring the husband

links.note: Rudradattan counts the konrai-wearing god's taking the mountain-daughter as his half as a stain and a great blame; Tirumanthiram 16 names the same god by that half-woman form as the one the gods delight in.
links.teaches: The same mark of Siva, his body shared with Uma, is a counsellor's example of lust's disgrace in a Jain epic and a title of praise in Tirumular's invocation, so the image itself is where the schools part.

gains.a: the counsellor's slight is seen to strike at a form the Saiva poets hold central
gains.b: the invocation's epithet is shown to be one a rival tradition read as a scandal

links.note: Rudradattan argues that lust's blame cannot be hidden and is drummed through the world; Naladiyar 89 says lust burns the mind itself, worse than fire or sun.
links.teaches: The counsellor argues from public disgrace and the quatrain from inward burning, so a reader sees that the ethics of desire had two separate arguments and that the epic, speaking to a king, chose reputation.

gains.a: the counsellor's choice of argument by reputation stands out against an argument he did not use
gains.b: the quatrain's inward harm is set beside the outward cost it leaves out

source_issues: 210: the identity of வாமனார் and the story told cannot be fixed from the verse.
209: the sense of the kurundu tree episode in lines 3-4 is unclear from the verse alone.
218: line 3 அறவு ஆக்கிய is hard to construe; possibly a corrupt reading.
Cast tamil விசயை follows the earlier chapter file; verse 201 spells the name விசையை.
